step1_summary: Chief complaint: Acute onset watery diarrhoea for the past 3 days.

Symptoms: • Frequency 5–6 loose, watery bowel motions/day • Began with 2 episodes of vomiting that have resolved • Mild subjective fever only on day 1, now afebrile • Feels very weak and dehydrated • No abdominal pain, no visible blood or mucus in stool • Poor oral intake, minimal appetite • No recent sick contacts or recalled high-risk food.
Past medical history: Mild intermittent asthma.
Medications/allergies: Uses blue salbutamol inhaler PRN; no other drugs; no known drug allergies.
Family history: Father – hypertension and died of bowel (colorectal) cancer at 58 y; Mother – type 2 diabetes.
Social history: Lives alone; software engineer; non-smoker; drinks alcohol socially, infrequently.
Vital signs / physical exam: Telephone consult – no vitals or exam findings provided.
Labs / imaging: None performed or mentioned.

V: Ischaemic colitis: Acute bloody or watery diarrhoea may follow transient colonic hypoperfusion, but patient lacks pain and risk factors.
I: Viral gastroenteritis (e.g., norovirus): Commonest cause of brief, self-limited watery diarrhoea with initial vomiting.
Bacterial food-borne infection (Salmonella, Campylobacter, ETEC): Can give 3-5 days of watery diarrhoea ± vomiting; no blood reported.
Giardiasis: Watery diarrhoea and bloating after contaminated water/travel (not reported but possible).
N: Colorectal carcinoma: Can present with altered bowel habit, but acute 3-day watery diarrhoea without blood or weight loss makes this less likely.
D: Lactase deficiency (lactose intolerance): Watery diarrhoea after dairy; no food trigger given, acute onset less typical.
I2: Clostridioides difficile infection: Antibiotic-associated or healthcare exposure—neither present, but still a potential infectious aetiology.
C: Congenital enzyme deficiencies (e.g., sucrase-isomaltase deficit) – lifelong, not acute.
A: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn’s/UC): Can flare with diarrhoea; blood and chronic course usually present, but initial loose stools possible.
T: Post-traumatic mesenteric injury causing bowel ischaemia—no trauma history.
E: Hyperthyroidism: Can cause diarrhoea and weight loss, but other systemic signs absent.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic triad of abrupt onset vomiting followed by 2–3 days of frequent watery diarrhoea, mild self-limited fever, no blood or severe pain, and spontaneous improvement expected.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis (Salmonella, Campylobacter, ETEC, Staph toxin)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Similar time-frame (3–5 days) and symptoms; can occur without obvious food recall; usually more systemic upset or abdominal cramps but overlaps with presentation.
Watery diarrhoea possible, but absence of recent antibiotics, hospitalisation, or characteristic foul odour makes this less probable.
Family history of colorectal pathology and patient age make IBD possible, but sudden brief illness without chronic or bloody diarrhoea argues against.
Could cause acute diarrhoea in older patients but normally painful, often bloody, and associated with vascular risk factors.

supporting_evidence: Sudden onset vomiting then watery diarrhoea
Duration 3 days, typical of viral course
Frequency 5–6/day without blood or severe pain
No recent antibiotics or chronic disease
opposing_evidence: No known sick contacts or obvious food source (but not required)
Subjective mild fever only (although viruses can be afebrile)

supporting_evidence: Watery diarrhoea 3-day course could match Salmonella/Campylobacter/ETEC
Initial vomiting can occur with toxin-mediated food poisoning
opposing_evidence: Patient does not recall suspect meal or travel
Lack of abdominal cramping, blood, or high fever that often accompany bacterial causes
No antibiotic use or hospital exposure

supporting_evidence: Age (48) within range for late IBD presentation
Family history of colorectal cancer may raise general lower GI risk awareness
opposing_evidence: No chronicity; only 3 days of symptoms
No blood, mucus, weight loss, or abdominal pain
No abdominal pain, typically colicky or crampy in ischaemia
No blood per rectum, common in ischaemic cases
Patient lacks vascular risk factors (smoking, AF, atherosclerosis)
